pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 🧩 **Strand 4 — Computational Thinking**
Sub-strand 1: Introduction to Programming

Programs are built from constants, variables, expressions and statements combined with operators. In this unit you will see how familiar classroom mathematics is written in code.

pages.title: Constants, Variables, Expressions, Statements and Operators
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.4.1.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- describe the basic concepts in programming;
- compare mathematical notation with coding notation.
| **Concept** | **Meaning** | **Python example** |
|---|---|---|
| Constant | A value that does not change | VAT = 0.15 |
| Variable | A named storage location whose value can change | price = 120 |
| Expression | A combination of values, variables and operators that produces a value | price ∗ VAT |
| Statement / instruction | A complete line of code that performs an action | total = price + price ∗ VAT |
| Assignment statement | Stores a value in a variable (uses = in Python, ← in pseudocode) | count = count + 1 |
| Arithmetic operators | Perform calculations | + - ∗ / // % ∗∗ |
| Relational (comparison) operators | Compare values; give True or False | == != > < >= <= |
| Logical operators | Combine conditions | and or not |
| Operator precedence | The order in which operators are evaluated | Brackets, then ∗, then / // %, then + - |

pages.title: Constants, Variables, Expressions, Statements and Operators (continued)
pages.body:
> 🧪 **Activity — Classroom mathematics vs coding**
Copy and complete the comparison table in your notebook. It shows how the same notation is written in classroom mathematics, Python, Scratch and Excel.
| **Operation** | **Classroom maths** | **Python** | **Scratch** | **Excel** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Addition | 7 + 3 | 7 + 3 | ( 7 ) + ( 3 ) | =7+3 |
| Subtraction | 7 − 3 | 7 - 3 | ( 7 ) - ( 3 ) | =7-3 |
| Multiplication | 7 × 3 | 7 ∗ 3 | ( 7 ) ∗ ( 3 ) | =7∗3 |
| Division | 7 ÷ 3 | 7 / 3 → 2.333… | ( 7 ) / ( 3 ) | =7/3 |
| Whole-number division | 7 ÷ 3 = 2 r 1 | 7 // 3 → 2 | floor of (7/3) | =QUOTIENT(7,3) |
| Remainder | remainder of 7 ÷ 3 | 7 % 3 → 1 | ( 7 ) mod ( 3 ) | =MOD(7,3) |
| Power | 7² | 7 ∗∗ 2 → 49 | — | =7^2 |
| Equal to | a = b | a == b | ( a ) = ( b ) | =A1=B1 |
| Not equal to | a ≠ b | a != b | not (a = b) | =A1<>B1 |
| Less than or equal | a ≤ b | a <= b | (a < b) or (a = b) | =A1<=B1 |
| Greater than or equal | a ≥ b | a >= b | (a > b) or (a = b) | =A1>=B1 |
> 🎯 **BECE focus — Equals in maths vs equals in code** In mathematics, x = x + 1 is impossible. In programming, x = x + 1 is an **assignment**: “take the current value of x, add 1, and store the result back in x.” To **test** equality, Python uses ==.
> ✏️ **Worked example — Logical operators**
age = 14 and has_ticket = True
age >= 13 and has_ticket → **True** (both conditions true)
age < 12 or has_ticket → **True** (at least one true)
not has_ticket → **False**

pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. Distinguish between an expression and a statement, with examples.
2. Write Python expressions for: (a) 5 × 4 + 6; (b) the remainder when 25 is divided by 4; (c) 3 to the power 4.
3. Explain the difference between = and == in Python.
